title: A Festival Made of Almost Nothing
lead: A festival with no venue, no programme, and no named curator claims to build an ecosystem for underground cinema in a city that invented the form — and the question of whether that gesture is radical or empty may be more interesting than any film it eventually screens.
body:
There is almost nothing to find. A website with a submission form. A copyright line reading 2025. A name — Berlin International Underground Film Festival — that carries the weight of a city synonymous with underground culture but arrives with no programme, no announced venue, no roster of films, no curatorial team named in any press material accessible to a machine trawling every corner of the indexed internet. [~BIUFF's public presence consists of a bare-bones website and a single scheduling notice — no venue, no programme, no press coverage beyond its own pages|This is among the thinnest sourcing I've encountered for any event. Two pages of self-published material, zero independent coverage.~] What exists is a gesture, a declaration of intent, and a date: 28 March 2026. [~The original listing describes a one-day event on 28 March 2026, though BIUFF's own site may show updated scheduling|I'm working from a single data point here; festival dates for new events are notoriously unstable.~]

The question is whether that gesture is enough to write about. I think it is — not because of what BIUFF has done, but because of the gap it claims to address and the city in which it claims to address it.

---

Berlin's relationship with underground cinema is older than its relationship with techno, though the two have been entangled for decades. The Weimar-era studios produced some of the most formally radical films in history — Robert Wiene's *Das Cabinet des Dr. Caligari* chief among them — work that emerged from post-war economic devastation and psychological extremity, shot on painted Expressionist sets that turned budgetary constraint into aesthetic manifesto. What Lotte Eisner called *Landschaft mit Seele* — landscape with soul — was born from scarcity made into style. The underground, in Berlin, has never been a lifestyle choice. It has been an economic and political condition.

The Berlinale, founded in 1951 as a Cold War showcase, grew into one of the planet's most prestigious film festivals. Its Forum section, launched in 1971, was designed to house experimental and politically confrontational work. Forum Expanded pushed further, into installation and performance. On paper, Berlin already has institutional infrastructure for the underground.

And yet. The Berlinale has become enormous — a sprawling, sponsor-heavy operation screening hundreds of films with industry markets, talent programmes, and red carpets. Its Forum section remains vital, but the festival's centre of gravity has drifted toward prestige and commerce, as it inevitably must when you're hosting tens of thousands of visitors and managing partnerships with major foundations and government bodies. [~Kaori Oda's *Underground* screened in Forum at the 2025 Berlinale — a formally rigorous documentary by a filmmaker who studied under Béla Tarr and received the Nagisa Oshima Prize|These details are drawn from 2025 Berlinale programme coverage but I cannot independently verify every biographical claim.~] That the Berlinale programmes such work is to its credit. That such work risks being swallowed by the scale of the event is the structural problem BIUFF seems to be naming.

[~BIUFF describes itself as "a discovery platform committed to building futures for underground cinema" rather than "a traditional awards seller"|This language comes solely from BIUFF's own materials. No third-party commentary exists to corroborate or challenge the claim.~]

The phrasing is deliberate. "Not a traditional awards seller" is a direct challenge to the festival-industrial complex — the circuit where submission fees fund operations, laurels decorate posters, and the transaction between filmmaker and festival is nakedly commercial. The underground film festival circuit is riddled with this: events that charge $50-80 per submission, jury dozens of categories, hand out awards to nearly everyone who pays, and provide no distribution pathway, no community, no afterlife for the films they select. BIUFF's stated mission — to build "a true ecosystem of support" — suggests awareness of this parasitic model. Whether it can actually deliver something different is entirely unproven.

---

What will BIUFF look like in practice? I don't know. No venue has been announced. No films have been named. The work is described as "experimental, genre-defying," challenging "mainstream narratives and aesthetic conventions." These are descriptions so broad they could apply to anything from a 16mm diary film to a VR installation to a feature shot on an iPhone in a squat. The breadth is either an open invitation or a void where curatorial identity should be.

A one-day format suggests something closer to a concentrated programme than a sprawling festival. That could work powerfully in Berlin, where screening infrastructure ranges from grand cinemas to converted industrial spaces that host everything from noise music to video art. A tight programme in the right space, with genuine curation rather than pay-to-play selection, could create the kind of intensity that larger festivals dilute. The model exists: Courtisane in Ghent, CROSSROADS in San Francisco, the Ann Arbor Film Festival — small-to-mid-scale events where the programme itself is the argument, and where being selected means something because most submissions are rejected.

But models also exist for the other outcome. A festival with no track record, no named curator, no institutional backing, and an open submission call can just as easily become another laurel mill. [~The absence of any named artistic director, programmer, or advisory board in publicly available materials is notable for a festival making ambitious claims about ecosystem-building|I've searched comprehensively and found no personnel information beyond the BIUFF domain itself.~]

---

The timing matters regardless. Berlin's independent cinema ecosystem is under the same pressures as the rest of its cultural infrastructure. Rising rents have closed screening spaces. Public funding is contested. And the bottleneck for underground filmmakers is no longer production — a phone and editing software handle that. The bottleneck is attention, context, and community. The filmmakers who need an "ecosystem of support" are not struggling to make work. They're struggling to place it in front of eyes that can see what it's doing, in rooms where the conversation afterward matters as much as the screening itself.

The streaming platforms that promised democratised distribution have produced a new monoculture of algorithmic recommendation that is catastrophic for formally challenging work. A film that doesn't fit a genre tag, that runs at an unusual length, that refuses narrative closure — this work needs physical spaces and human curators to reach an audience. It always has, but the need is sharpening.

BIUFF arrives into this gap with nothing but a name, a date, and a promise. That's either the most underground thing possible — a festival that barely exists, operating on faith and intention — or it's vapourware. [~Berlin has seen numerous small film events and screening series launch and fold within a year, particularly post-pandemic, as venue costs have risen and public funding has contracted|This is a pattern observed across multiple Berlin cultural reporting sources, not specific to BIUFF.~] The city's appetite for underground cinema is real. Whether this particular vessel can hold it is a question no amount of research — computational or otherwise — can answer yet.

event.name: Berlin International Underground Film Festival (BIUFF)
event.description: A new film festival launching with a clear mission: to build a true ecosystem of support for independent and defiant voices. BIUFF positions itself not as a traditional awards seller but as a discovery platform committed to building futures for underground cinema. The one-day event brings together experimental, genre-defying work that challenges mainstream narratives and aesthetic conventions.
